item.title: Hagi Castle Town: Samurai Streets and Meiji History — Guide
item.description: Hagi is one of Japan’s best-preserved castle towns, a quiet grid of streets on the Sea of Japan coast where whole quarters of samurai and merchant houses survive behind long earthen walls, summer oranges hanging over the lanes. Once the castle seat of the powerful Mori clan, Hagi became a cradle of the Meiji Restoration, the movement that overthrew the shogunate and founded modern Japan — its private academy schooled several of the new nation’s founding leaders, and the town’s industrial heritage sites are UNESCO-listed.

item.title: Kitsuki Castle Town — Guide
item.description: Kitsuki is a beautifully preserved castle town on the Kunisaki Peninsula, often called Japan’s smallest castle town — and one of its most atmospheric. It has a distinctive ‘sandwich’ layout: two samurai districts sit on hills to the north and south, with a merchant district in the valley between them, linked by charming stone-paved slopes (the photogenic Suya-no-saka and Shioya-no-saka). Strolling the preserved streets, lined with samurai residences, earthen walls, old shops and gates, feels like stepping back into the Edo period.

item.title: Tsuwano: The 'Little Kyoto' of the San'in Hills — Guide
item.description: Tsuwano is a small, exquisitely preserved former castle town tucked in a valley in the far west of Shimane, often called a ‘Little Kyoto’ of the San’in region. Its signature is Tonomachi street, where the stone-lined water channels that run alongside the old white-walled samurai houses and merchant storehouses are famously filled with thousands of brightly coloured carp — so many that the fish are said to outnumber the townspeople. Above the town, the ruined stone ramparts of Tsuwano Castle crown a steep hill reached by chairlift, and the whole place has an unhurried, literary atmosphere far from the crowds.

item.title: Yamatokoriyama: Japan's Goldfish Town — Guide
item.description: Yamatokoriyama, a castle town just southwest of Nara, is famous across Japan as a capital of ornamental goldfish, bred here for some 300 years since samurai took up the hobby in the Edo period. Today goldfish are woven right into the town’s identity: rows of breeding ponds shimmer on its outskirts, goldfish motifs decorate the streets, and playful touches — goldfish in an old telephone booth, goldfish vending machines and shop displays — turn a stroll into a treasure hunt.

item.title: Gujo Hachiman: A Historic Water Town of Clear Streams — Guide
item.description: Gujo Hachiman is a historic castle town in central Gifu famous for its exceptionally clear water, with canals, springs and streams threaded through the old streets, small waterways running beside houses, and a culture built around treasuring and using the pure water in daily life. Above the town sits a small reconstructed mountain castle with valley views, while the streets below are lined with traditional houses, sweet shops and workshops, and the town is especially renowned for the Gujo Odori, a lively folk dance held over many summer nights.
